entities.name: Boganda National Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Boganda National Museum (French: Musée National Boganda) in Bangui, Central African Republic — named for Barthélemy Boganda (1910-1959), the founder of the Central African Republic and one of Africa's most important anti-colonial political figures — is the national museum of the Central African Republic, preserving materials related to the pre-colonial cultures of the Central African region, colonial history, and the independence movement that Boganda led before his death in a plane crash on the eve of independence.

Barthélemy Boganda was an extraordinary figure in African colonial history: the son of a Mbaka commoner who became the first ordained Central African Catholic priest (1938), he evolved from a religious figure to a radical anti-colonial political leader who founded the Movement for the Social Evolution of Black Africa (MESAN) and envisioned not just Central African independence but a federated 'United States of Latin Africa' combining the French Equatorial African territories. His 1959 death in a plane crash (the circumstances of which remain disputed, with some suspecting French colonial interests) occurred days before the independence he had worked toward.

The museum named for Boganda honors his legacy as the founding father of the Central African Republic while preserving pre-colonial cultural heritage from a region with exceptionally rich but poorly documented traditional cultures. The Central African Republic's complex post-independence history — multiple coups, civil wars, and one of the world's most challenging humanitarian situations — makes cultural heritage preservation an urgent priority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Boganda National Museum CAR — named for Barthélemy Boganda, one of Africa's most visionary anti-colonial leaders who died before achieving independence, and preserving Central African cultural heritage in one of the world's most challenging political environments — is historically significant as a monument to African anti-colonialism and cultural resilience.
